claim_text: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 randomized trials found that apparent pooled improvements in skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkles were not present in analyses restricted to trials without pharmaceutical-company funding or to high-quality studies; the authors concluded that clinical evidence does not support collagen supplements to prevent or treat skin aging.
health_goal_or_outcome: Oral collagen supplementation for prevention or treatment of skin aging.

population.age_range: Adults represented in included randomized trials; exact range varies by study.
population.sex_or_life_stage: Mixed trial populations; not a pregnancy/lactation assessment.
population.health_status: General populations studied for skin aging.
population.other_context: 23 RCTs, 1,474 participants; studies searched through June 14, 2024.

ingredient_form_or_preparation: Oral collagen supplements; formulations and sources varied across trials.
comparator: Placebo or control conditions in included randomized trials.
evidence_summary: Myung and Park, American Journal of Medicine 2025;138(9):1264–1277. DOI 10.1016/j.amjmed.2025.04.034. Funding-source and study-quality subgroup analyses materially changed the interpretation of pooled findings.
limitations: This single review does not resolve all collagen indications, such as joint outcomes.
Do not generalize the skin-aging conclusion to every collagen product or outcome.
Formal GRADE appraisal has not yet been completed.
